title: Emergency Services
subtitle: How PSTN2 gives 999 and 112 call handlers the caller’s current location in milliseconds, instead of yesterday’s batch file.
endNote: Real-time caller location, from every participating provider, for every emergency call.

segments.text: When someone calls 999 or 112, every second counts.
Responders need to know exactly where the caller is, straight away.
Lives depend on finding people quickly.
Yet today’s systems often give them location data that is out of date, or too vague to act on.
Today’s emergency location system relies on batch updates.
Providers send their location records to the emergency services about once every 24 hours.
So the data can be up to a day old.
If a customer’s details changed recently, the emergency services receive the wrong information.
Current systems often place a caller only within a postcode area, which can cover several square kilometres.
In a town or city, that can take in dozens of buildings.
Responders lose precious time searching for the right one.
In rural areas, the problem is even worse.
PSTN2 replaces the batch file with a real-time location query.
When a 999 call arrives, the emergency call centre asks the caller’s provider for the device’s location, at that moment.
The answer includes GPS coordinates when they are available, typically accurate to within fifteen metres.
Current data, in milliseconds.
A 999 call arrives. The number dialled is enough to mark it as an emergency.
To find the caller’s provider, the call centre uses PSTN2 number discovery: its cache, then Ofcom’s numbering list, then the Range Holder.
This caller’s number was ported, so the Range Holder redirects to Bravo Networks. The answer is cached for next time.
The call centre sends Bravo a signed location request. Only registered emergency centres can ask.
Bravo checks its live records and answers within milliseconds, with the most recent location it has.
For a mobile phone, the location can draw on several sources.
GPS satellites, typically accurate to between five and fifteen metres.
Nearby Wi-Fi access points, to within about twenty to fifty metres.
And the serving cell, to within a hundred metres to a kilometre.
The provider gathers these from the device and sends the best available, in real time. Not from yesterday’s batch file.
Even for fixed lines, PSTN2 improves accuracy.
Today, the emergency services may receive an address from a database that is a year out of date.
With PSTN2, the provider answers from its live records: a recently verified billing address, and its installation records.
Plus any location the customer has confirmed. All of it up to date, at the moment of the call.
Real-time location can cut emergency response times by minutes.
Studies show that in cardiac arrest, every minute of delay reduces the chance of survival by around ten percent.
Faster response translates directly into lives saved.
Regulators already expect accurate, real-time caller location.
The EU’s eCall system for vehicles, Enhanced 911 in the United States, and Advanced Mobile Location in the UK all point the same way.

segments.text: PSTN2 goes further. It provides the infrastructure to deliver real-time location from every participating provider, for every call.
